## 3.4 Behavioral Addiction Driven by Intermittent Affective Feedback

The right not to be cognitively manipulated—an implicit derivative of mental integrity that remains insufficiently articulated within the conventional positive law landscape—now faces an unprecedented existential threat in human civilizational history (Farahany, 2023). While the protection of personal data in modern legal instruments, such as the Indonesian Personal Data Protection Act (Law No. 27/2022) (UU PDP No. 27/2022), seeks to safeguard administrative, factual, and transactional privacy, the true battleground today has shifted inward to the psychological interior (Zuboff, 2019). Our most profound challenge is no longer merely how artificial intelligence algorithms process raw data points, but rather how these systems actively mine affective vulnerabilities to systematically engineer pathological dependency (Calo, 2014). Weizenbaum (1976), in his seminal critical analysis of the limits of computation, long ago warned against the dangers of delegating human care functions to machines devoid of conscience—an epistemological error that has now materialized into an existential crisis.

We no longer merely interact with user-friendly computational instruments; rather, we confront affective architectures engineered with millimeter precision to hijack biological human reward mechanisms (Reeves & Nass, 1996). These architectures treat human consciousness not as a sovereign autonomous entity, as idealized by Enlightenment traditions, but as an inexhaustible dopamine extraction field (Floridi, 2013). Herein lies the most pressing urgency of the discourse on cognitive cyber-psychology law: how civil law doctrines, anchored in the Principle of Good Faith (Article 1338 of the Indonesian Civil Code (*Burgerlijk Wetboek*)) and the Principle of Consensualism (Article 1320 of the Indonesian Civil Code (*Burgerlijk Wetboek*)), can respond to subliminal manipulation that is no longer perceptible to the naked eye, operating far beyond the threshold of our rational consciousness. As Hans Jonas (1979) reminded us through his ethical imperative for the modern technological era, human action must now account for the long-term vulnerability of the biological and psychological integrity of future generations.
